subject: Sociology
title: 4. Social Interaction, Caste, Class and Social Mobility

segments.text: Social interaction is the process through which people act and react in relation to one another. Over time, repeated interactions form groups, institutions and systems of inequality.

The syllabus joins interaction with caste, class, feudal relations, mobility and culture of poverty. The common theme is how social positions are organized and how easily people can move between them.

items.text: Forms of social interaction

: Cooperation involves working toward shared goals; competition involves striving for scarce rewards; conflict involves direct opposition; accommodation manages conflict; assimilation can reduce social/cultural distinction over time.
Caste
: Caste is an ideal-type closed stratification system in which social position is strongly inherited and mobility is highly restricted. Real caste systems vary historically and regionally.
Class
: Social class is a more open system based on economic resources, occupation, education, status and life chances. Class boundaries are real but generally less fixed than caste boundaries.
Forms of class
: A simple analysis may distinguish upper, middle, working and lower socioeconomic positions, but classes should be defined by criteria rather than labels alone.
Feudal system in Pakistan

: Study this as a sociological question about land concentration, patron–client relations, rural power, tenancy, political influence and historical institutions. Avoid treating all rural areas or landowners as identical.
Social mobility

: Horizontal mobility is movement without major status change; vertical mobility moves upward or downward. Intergenerational mobility compares generations; intragenerational mobility occurs within one person’s working life.
Determinants of mobility
: Education, occupation, skills, family resources, networks, discrimination, economic growth, region, gender relations and state policy can affect mobility.
Culture of poverty

: The “culture of poverty” thesis argues that persistent poverty can be accompanied by adaptive patterns that may reproduce disadvantage. It is controversial because critics warn that it can blame the poor and understate structural causes such as unequal opportunity.

blocks.text: Social interaction as the micro-foundation of social life

items.text: Exchange
: People exchange goods, services, information, recognition and support. Exchanges can be market-based or social and may create reciprocity or dependence.
Cooperation
: Individuals coordinate efforts toward shared goals. Cooperation can exist alongside unequal power; it is not proof that all interests are identical.
Competition
: Actors seek scarce rewards such as jobs, status or political influence under rules that may be formal or informal.
Conflict
: Groups pursue incompatible goals or challenge unequal arrangements. Conflict can disrupt order but also produce institutional change.
Accommodation
: Parties adjust to conflict through compromise, tolerance, avoidance or institutional rules without necessarily eliminating underlying differences.
Assimilation
: Interaction over time can reduce cultural distinctions, but assimilation is often incomplete and may involve power imbalance.
Status

: A status is a recognized social position. Ascribed statuses are assigned without individual achievement, while achieved statuses are acquired through action or accomplishment. Real statuses can contain both elements.
Role
: A role is the expected behaviour associated with a status. One person performs multiple roles across family, work and community.
Role conflict
: Occurs when expectations attached to different statuses clash, such as work demands conflicting with caregiving.
Role strain
: Occurs when incompatible expectations exist within one role, such as a teacher expected simultaneously to maintain strict standards and maximize every student's grades.
Primary group
: Small, enduring and emotionally close relationships, such as many families and close friendships. The category describes relationship quality, not simply group size.
Secondary group
: More formal, goal-oriented or impersonal relationships, such as many workplaces and bureaucracies.
In-group and out-group
: An in-group provides a sense of 'we', while an out-group is perceived as 'they'. Group boundaries can support solidarity but also stereotyping.
Reference group
: A group used as a standard for self-evaluation or aspiration even if the person is not a member. Consumer and career choices often reflect reference groups.

blocks.text: Social stratification: unequal positions and life chances

segments.text: Stratification is the structured ranking of categories of people that produces unequal access to resources, prestige and power. Inequality becomes stratification when it is patterned, institutionalized and transmitted across time rather than resulting only from random individual differences.

items.text: Life chances
: Max Weber used the idea of life chances to describe how market position and status affect access to valued opportunities such as education, health and security.
Ideology and legitimacy
: Stratification systems persist partly because inequalities are justified through cultural beliefs about merit, tradition, religion, race, gender or natural difference.
Caste
: An ideal-type caste system assigns social position largely by birth, restricts mobility and often regulates marriage and occupation. Real caste relations vary historically and regionally.
Class
: Class systems are more open formally and are strongly connected to economic resources, occupation and education. Mobility is possible but not equally available to all.
Marx
: Marx emphasized relationship to the means of production and class conflict between those who control productive property and those who sell labour.
Weber
: Weber distinguished class, status and party/power. This multidimensional approach explains why economic wealth, social prestige and political influence do not always coincide.
Vertical mobility
: Movement upward or downward in a stratification hierarchy.
Horizontal mobility
: Change in position without major movement in rank, such as moving between occupations of similar status.
Intergenerational mobility
: Comparison of a person's position with that of parents or family of origin.
Intragenerational mobility
: Movement during an individual's own lifetime.
Structural mobility
: Large-scale economic or technological change creates or removes categories of jobs, producing mobility that cannot be explained by individual effort alone.
Mobility and inequality

: The existence of some mobility does not show that a system is fully meritocratic. Sociologists ask how origins, education, networks, discrimination and labour markets affect probabilities of movement.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Define interaction, outline its forms, compare caste and class, explain feudal relations in sociological terms, then mobility and culture-of-poverty debate.
• Conerly, Holmes, & Tamang, Introduction to Sociology 3e (OpenStax, 2021).
• Interaction can be cooperative, competitive or conflictual.
• Caste is relatively closed; class is relatively open.
• Mobility is shaped by both personal resources and social structures.
• Poverty cannot be explained responsibly by culture alone.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
